newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Fujimori rules out use of force in hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori rules out use of force in hostage crisis.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, in Bolivia for crisis talks with Bolivian leader Sanchez de Lozada, on Saturday ruled out again the use of force to free the 72 VIPs held hostage by Marxist rebels.

"The use of force is a move which would become the last (resource), in case of an incontrollable emergency which we hope will not come about," he told a joint news conference after talks with Sanchez de Lozada.

The Bolivian leader said his government could not bow to Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels' demands for freedom for their four comrades in Bolivia, echoing Fujimori's own stand on the 450 MRTA prisoners in Peruvian jails.

The MRTA has been holding Bolivian ambassador Jorge Gumucio, Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki, two Peruvian government ministers and scores of dignitaries, including two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen at Aoki's residence in Lima since Dec. 17.

The rebels have offered to free Gumucio in exchange for the release of their four comrades jailed in Bolivia. But Sanchez de Lozada said the rebels were in the hands of Bolivian judges and outside his jurisdiction.
"There is no way that under our legal system the executive branch can take a decision about it."
Looking taciturn, avoiding questions and giving few details, Fujimori said no efforts were being spared to find a negotiated solution to the 109-day crisis.
Sanchez de Lozada said he was concerned by the deadlock in talks to solve Latin America's longest hostage siege, but he trusted Lima and Tokyo would find a peaceful way out.
"It is a delicate situation, anything can happen," he told reporters. "But we are encouraged by the positions of Japan and Peru."
Fujimori said the three countries, which have kept in constant touch on the crisis, were in full agreement about the way things were being handled.

The Peruvian leader could not confirm reports that Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, member of a three-man mediation team, visited a naval base in the port of Callao where MRTA leader Victor Polay and other MRTA leaders are held.

He said he would get in touch with naval authorities to find out about the reports, which triggered speculation in Lima that Cipriani, facing an impasse in talks with MRTA fighters inside the residence, was taking negotiations directly to the MRTA leadership.
Fujimori, grappling with the greatest challenge to his authority since taking office in 1990, arrived in Santa Cruz late on Friday and went directly into talks with Sanchez de Lozada.

On Saturday they had a working breakfast and held a joint news conference before heading for the coca-producing Chapare area. Officials said the fight against drugs and plans for an Andean summit in Sucre, Bolivia, in late April were also on their agenda.
At the besieged residence in Lima's wealthy San Isidro district, police continued to query curious onlookers and reporters who strayed too close to the house.
A Peruvian photographer for Agence France-Presse, Cristobal Bouroncle, was briefly detained by police near the residence allegedly for not carrying the proper credentials.

A secret intelligence report obtained by Reuters said new information suggested Congress President Victor Joy Way, two legislators and five mayors -- all harsh critics of the MRTA -- might be targeted for attacks by rebel commandos.
Joy Way was expected to fly to Tokyo this month for hostage crisis talks with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
